title: Investigation: Structure and Function Comparison

opener.title: Investigation: Structure and Function Comparison
opener.question: Why do birds have so many different beak shapes? Can a beak's shape decide what a bird is able to eat?
opener.alt: An opening film that zooms in from Earth seen from space, to the Galápagos Islands, to the tiny island of Daphne Major, to a ground finch on dry ground, to a close-up of a finch's thick beak, and finally to the hard, spiny fruits finches crack open.

k-warmup.text: Four birds, four foods, but the foods are in the wrong spots. Swap them until each food sits under the beak built to eat it. Then pick which tool you think will win with beans, and which will win with rice. Tap Save my guess, and write why.

k-words.text: Beak. Structure. Function. Fair test. Data. Environment.

k-part1.text: In eighteen forty-five, Charles Darwin printed this page about the finches he saw on the Galápagos Islands. Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English. Then slide the caliper jaws, and measure each beak.

k-quiz.text: Three quick questions, just for you. They are not graded. Tap an answer and read the note under it. Think about what job each structure does.

k-assign.text: Now write your half of page twenty. Answer the two Part B questions. In Part C, make your beak data card. Then tap evidence cards in the planner to build your C-E-R about how beak shapes help birds survive.

menu.title: Swap the menu

job: Tap a food, then tap another food to swap them.
Or drag one food onto another.
Put each food under the beak built to eat it, then tap Check my menu.

beaks.name: Large ground finch
beaks.alt: A brown-gray finch on a rock, with a short, thick, cone-shaped beak.
beaks.hint: A short, thick beak is strong, like a nutcracker. Which food has to be cracked?
beaks.why: A thick beak cracks hard seeds.

beaks.name: Great blue heron
beaks.alt: The head of a gray heron with a long, sharp, pointed yellow beak.
beaks.hint: A long, sharp beak works like a spear. Which food swims?
beaks.why: A long, sharp beak grabs fish in the water.

beaks.name: Red-tailed hawk
beaks.alt: The head of a brown hawk with a short, hooked, sharp beak.
beaks.hint: A hooked beak tears meat. Which food is a small animal?

beaks.name: Ruby-throated hummingbird
beaks.alt: A tiny green hummingbird hovering by purple flowers, with a long, thin beak.
beaks.hint: A long, thin beak works like a straw. Which food is a sweet liquid hidden in a flower?
beaks.why: A long, thin beak sips nectar from deep in a flower.

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to see what it means.

words.def: The hard mouth part of a bird. Its shape decides what foods the bird can eat.
A body part of a living thing, like a beak, a root, or a shell.
The job a structure does. A beak's function is to get food.
A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
Numbers and facts you collect during a test. Data helps you compare results.
The place where an organism lives, including its food, water, and weather.

source.title: Darwin's finches
source.alt: Two printed pages in English from Darwin's 1845 book. The left page, page 379, has a drawing of four finch heads with beaks from very thick to very thin. The right page, page 380, is all text.
source.intro: In 1835, a 26-year-old scientist named Charles Darwin visited the Galápagos Islands on a ship called the Beagle. He collected birds, including many finches. Ten years later, in 1845, he printed these two pages in his book Journal of Researches.
job: Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English.
Then find the two lines in the hunts.

lines.en: The other land birds are a very unusual group of finches. They are related to each other by the shape of their beaks, their short tails, their bodies and their feathers. There are thirteen kinds.
Most of these finches gather in flocks and feed on the dry, bare ground of the lowlands.
The strangest fact is that the beak sizes change in perfect steps, from a beak as big as a hawfinch's to one as small as a chaffinch's.
Darwin's drawing: four finch heads. Number 1 has the biggest, deepest beak. Numbers 3 and 4 have small, thin beaks.
Their names. Today we call them: 1, the large ground finch. 2, the medium ground finch. 3, the small tree finch. 4, the warbler finch.

The biggest beak is in Fig. 1 and the smallest in Fig. 3. But in between, there is not just one kind with a medium beak, like Fig. 2. There are at least six kinds, with beaks that change in tiny steps.
The warbler finch's thin beak is shown in Fig. 4. The cactus finch's beak is a bit like a starling's. Another group has a beak shaped a little like a parrot's.

Seeing these step-by-step beaks in one small group of closely related birds, you might really imagine this: long ago, when very few birds lived on these islands, one kind of bird arrived, and it was changed over time for different jobs.

asks.q: Hunt 1: Find the line where Darwin says the beak sizes change in perfect steps.
asks.yes: Yes! From big to small, in tiny steps. That is why you will measure them next.
asks.no: Not that one. Look at the left page, just above the drawing.

asks.q: Hunt 2: Find the line where Darwin wonders if one kind of bird was changed for different jobs.
asks.yes: Yes! Darwin wondered if one kind of finch arrived long ago and its beaks changed to fit different foods. That idea grew into his famous theory.
asks.no: Not quite. Look at the right page, about a third of the way down.

source.credit: Source: Charles Darwin, Journal of Researches into the Natural History and Geology of the Countries Visited during the Voyage of H.M.S. Beagle, 2nd edition (London: John Murray, 1845), pages 379 and 380, scan from the Wellcome Collection via the Internet Archive (public domain). Plain-English version written for this lesson.

caliper.title: Caliper check
caliper.intro: Scientists who study Darwin's finches today measure each beak with a tool called a caliper. Its two jaws close on the beak, and its scale shows how deep the beak is. Try it on Darwin's real drawing.
job: Drag the top jaw to the top of the beak, where it meets the feathers.
Drag the bottom jaw to the bottom of the beak.
Tap Read the caliper. Measure all four finches.
caliper.alt: Darwin's 1845 drawing of four finch heads, with a model caliper beside the beak you are measuring.

hints.topHigh: The top jaw is floating above the beak. Move it down until it just touches the top of the beak.
hints.topLow: The top jaw is pressing into the beak. Move it up to the top edge of the beak.
hints.botLow: The bottom jaw is below the beak. Move it up until it touches the bottom edge.
hints.botHigh: The bottom jaw is inside the beak. Move it down to the bottom edge.

caliper.ask: Look at your four readings. What pattern did Darwin notice?

opts.t: The beaks change in steps, from very deep seed-crackers to thin insect-pickers
All four beaks are about the same depth
opts.hint: Compare your biggest reading with your smallest. Are they close?

opts.t: The finches with thin beaks crack the biggest seeds
opts.hint: Think about a nutcracker and a pair of tweezers. Which one cracks hard things?

caliper.win: Right. Darwin called it a perfect gradation: big steps down, from the deep beak of Finch 1 to the thin beak of Finch 4. Each beak fits a different food.
caliper.againLabel: ↺ Open the caliper and measure again
caliper.credit: Drawing: Darwin, Journal of Researches (1845), page 379 (public domain). The caliper is a model; its units measure the drawing, not the real birds.

shadow.title: Shadow match
shadow.intro: Six real birds, six kitchen and workshop tools. Each beak works like one of these tools.
job: Pick a tool, then tap the bird whose beak works like it.
Or drag the tool onto the bird.

birds.name: Northern cardinal
birds.alt: A bright red cardinal with a short, thick, cone-shaped orange beak.
birds.why: Nutcracker! A cardinal's thick beak cracks seeds, like the ground finches on Darwin's page.
birds.hint: Look for a short, thick, strong beak.

birds.name: Sword-billed hummingbird
birds.alt: A green hummingbird perched on a branch, with a beak even longer than its body.
birds.meal: Eats: nectar from very long flowers
birds.why: Straw! This hummingbird's beak is longer than the rest of its body, so it reaches nectar no other bird can.
birds.hint: Look for the longest, thinnest beak.

birds.name: Great blue heron
birds.alt: A heron's head with a long, sharp, dagger-shaped yellow beak, by the sea in Florida.
birds.why: Spear! A heron stands still, then strikes fast with its sharp beak to grab a fish.
birds.hint: Look for a long, sharp beak like a dagger.

birds.name: Osprey
birds.alt: An osprey's head with a black, sharply hooked beak and a yellow eye.
birds.meal: Eats: fish it tears into bites
birds.why: Hook! An osprey's hooked beak tears meat into bites it can swallow.
birds.hint: Look for a beak that curves down to a sharp point.

birds.name: Northern shoveler
birds.alt: A duck with a green head and a very wide, flat, spoon-shaped bill, standing in shallow water.
birds.meal: Eats: tiny animals and seeds strained from water
birds.why: Strainer! A shoveler's wide bill has comb-like edges that strain tiny food out of muddy water.
birds.hint: Look for a wide, flat bill used in water.

birds.name: Pileated woodpecker
birds.alt: A black-and-white woodpecker with a red crest, clinging to a tree trunk, with a straight, pointed beak.
birds.why: Chisel! A woodpecker hammers its strong, pointed beak into wood to reach insects inside.
birds.hint: Look for a bird on a tree trunk with a strong, straight beak.

shadow.win: Six beaks, six tools. A beak's shape tells you its job.

plant.kicker: Part 2 · A plant structure that fits a beak
plant.title: Flowers have matching structures too

photos.alt: Coral-pink trumpet honeysuckle flowers, each a long, narrow tube.
photos.cap: Trumpet honeysuckle: each flower is a long, narrow tube.

photos.alt: A ruby-throated hummingbird hovering with its long beak in a red flower.
photos.cap: A ruby-throated hummingbird drinking from a tube-shaped flower.

plant.text: Trumpet honeysuckle grows wild in Florida. It keeps its nectar at the bottom of a long, narrow tube. A hummingbird's long, thin beak reaches the nectar. While it drinks, pollen rubs onto its head, and it carries that pollen to the next flower. The plant's tube and the bird's beak fit together.
plant.ask: How does the flower's long tube help the plant?

opts.t: Birds must push in close to reach the nectar, so pollen rubs off on them
The tube keeps hummingbirds away from the flower
opts.hint: Look at the second photo. Is the hummingbird kept away?

opts.t: The tube makes the plant grow taller
opts.hint: The tube is part of the flower. What visits the flower?

plant.win: Right. The flower's structure (a long tube) and the bird's structure (a long beak) help each other: the bird gets food, and the plant gets its pollen moved.
plant.credit: Photos: trumpet honeysuckle, Paul VanDerWerf (CC BY 2.0); hummingbird, Linda Tanner (CC BY 2.0).

flaw.kicker: Part 3 game · Is it a fair test?
flaw.title: Spot the flaw
flaw.intro: Four students wrote plans for the beak test. Three plans have one thing that makes the test unfair. One plan is fair.
job: Tap the part that makes the test unfair.
If nothing is wrong, tap This test is fair.

parts: I will give the spoon 60 seconds
I will start with 40 beans each time.
plans.why: Right. The spoon gets twice as much time, so it would move more beans even if it were a worse beak. Every tool needs the same time.

fine.1: 30 seconds is fine by itself. Compare it with the time the spoon gets.
fine.2: One hand is fair, as long as every tool uses one hand.
fine.3: Starting with the same 40 beans each time is fair.

parts: I will give every tool 30 seconds.
I will use two hands with the spoon
and one hand with the clothespin.
I will start with 40 beans each time.
plans.why: Right. Two hands is a big help. A bird has only one beak, so every tool gets one hand.

fine.0: The same 30 seconds for every tool is fair.
fine.2: One hand is right. Is that true for every tool?
fine.3: The same 40 beans each time is fair.

parts: I will give every tool 30 seconds
The spoon gets a pile of 40 beans,
plans.why: Right. With only 10 beans, the clothespin could never move more than 10. Every tool needs the same pile.

fine.2: 40 beans is fine. Does every tool get 40?

parts: I will give every tool 30 seconds,
and start with 40 beans each time.
plans.why: Right. Leo changes only one thing, the tool. Everything else stays the same. That is a fair test.

fine.2: That part is fair. Is anything in Leo's plan unfair?

flaw.notFair: Look again. Something in this plan changes besides the tool.
flaw.fineDefault: That part is fair. Look for the part that changes besides the tool.
flaw.win: In a fair test, you change only one thing (the tool) and keep everything else the same: the time, the hands, and the pile of food.

beaklab.cardIntro: Now test your Warm-Up guess. Your tools are the beaks. The beans and rice are the food.
beaklab.title: Three tools. Two foods. One fair test.
beaklab.intro: You will run six trials: each tool with beans, then each tool with rice. Every trial gets 30 seconds, one hand, and the same pile of food.
job: Choose real tools or the on-screen test.
Run all six trials and fill in the table.
Read your graph and compare it with your guess.
beaklab.safety: Don't eat any of the test food, and keep small beans away from little brothers and sisters.
beaklab.realLabel: 🥄 I have a spoon, tweezers, and a clothespin
beaklab.realSteps: Put a small pile of dry beans on one plate and a small pile of rice on another. Put an empty bowl next to each. Pick one tool, use one hand, tap Start, and move as much food as you can into the bowl. When the timer stops, count what is in the bowl and type the number in the table. Put the food back and repeat for every tool and food.
beaklab.screenSteps: Pick a tool and a food, then tap Start the trial. Tap the plate to grab food with the tool, then tap the bowl to drop it. Your count goes into the table when time runs out.
beaklab.plateAlt: A model of a plate of food and an empty blue bowl. Tap the plate to grab, tap the bowl to drop.
beaklab.holding: Holding {n}. Tap the bowl to drop.
beaklab.dropFirst: Drop what you are holding in the bowl first.
beaklab.slipLine: Oops, it slipped off! Try again.
beaklab.trialDone: Time! The {t} moved {n}. It is in your table.
beaklab.screenModel: A model: the beans, rice, plate and bowl are drawings, and each tool grabs the way a real one usually does.
beaklab.badNum: Type a whole number from 0 to {max}, like 12.
beaklab.graphAlt: A bar graph of your data: for each tool, one bar for beans and one bar for rice.
beaklab.compareTitle: Your Warm-Up guess vs. your data
beaklab.ask: A friend says: "The spoon is the best beak, because it picked up the most." What should a scientist check first?

opts.t: Which tool won each food, because a beak can be great for one food and poor for another

opts.hint: Does shine help a beak get food? Look at your data instead.

opts.t: Nothing. The tool that moved the most beans is best at everything
opts.hint: Look at the rice column. Does the same tool always win?

beaklab.win: Right. A scientist compares the tools one food at a time. The best tool for beans may not be the best tool for rice.

twist.head: There is no best beak. There is only the best beak for a food.
twist.line: Each food column can have its own winner. A shape that works well for one food can work poorly for another.
twist.chain: That is why Darwin's finches have different beaks: each beak fits the food that kind of finch eats.

beaklab.againLabel: ↺ Clear my table and test again

footage.title: A heron goes fishing
footage.intro: This great blue heron is standing still in a pond, watching the water. Watch what its beak does.
look: How long does the heron wait before it strikes?
Watch the beak at the end. What is in it?
Why is a long, sharp beak a good tool for this job?
footage.credit: Video: “Great Blue Heron Catching Fish at Colonel Samuel Smith Park”, Lucastphotography (CC BY 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons. Cut, cropped and muted for this lesson; the underwater part is sped up.

data.title: Finch beaks before and after a drought
data.intro: On Daphne Major in 1977, almost no rain fell, and most small seeds ran out. Only big, hard seeds were left. Scientists Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the beaks of medium ground finches before the drought (751 birds in 1976) and after it (89 birds in 1978). Each bar shows how many birds out of every 100 had a beak of that depth.
job: Drag across the bars to read each group.
Compare the gray bars (before) with the orange bars (after).

opts.t: More of the finches had deep beaks
More of the finches had thin beaks
opts.hint: Read the Under 9 mm group. Did it go up or down?
Compare 6.5 with 19 in the 11 mm or more group.

data.win: Right. Before the drought, only about 7 birds out of 100 had beaks 11 mm or deeper. After it, about 19 out of 100 did. Finches with deeper beaks could crack the hard seeds that were left, so more of them survived.
data.alt: A grouped bar graph of beak depth in medium ground finches. Under 9 mm: 22 before, 9 after. 9 to 10 mm: 41 before, 29 after. 10 to 11 mm: 30.5 before, 42.5 after. 11 mm or more: 6.5 before, 19 after (birds out of every 100).
data.credit: Data: beak depths of 751 medium ground finches caught on Daphne Major in 1976 and 89 caught in 1978, from Peter and Rosemary Grant's study (Grant, Ecology and Evolution of Darwin's Finches, Princeton University Press, 1986), as shared in the Sleuth3 data set ex0218 (Ramsey and Schafer). Downloaded 25 Nov 2026; percentages worked out for this lesson.

cabinet.title: Archaeopteryx: an early bird with teeth
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of a flat slab of stone with the skeleton of an early bird pressed into it, with its wings spread and long, bony tail.
cabinet.text: This is a 3D scan of a famous fossil found in Germany, called Archaeopteryx. It lived about 150 million years ago. Its jaws had small teeth, not a beak! It also had claws on its wings and a long, bony tail. Birds' beaks came later. Spin it, and find the wings and the tail.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Archaeopteryx siemensii, USNM PAL 509743, Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian (CC0).

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: In my beak test, the tool that moved the most beans was not always the tool that moved the most rice.
A thick beak, like a nutcracker, cracks hard seeds. A long, thin beak, like a straw, sips nectar from deep flowers.
Darwin's drawing shows finch beaks that change in steps, from very deep seed-crackers to thin insect-pickers.
A heron's long, sharp beak works like a spear to grab fish in shallow water.
After the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, more of the medium ground finches had deep beaks that could crack the hard seeds that were left.
Trumpet honeysuckle's long flower tube fits a hummingbird's long beak, so the bird gets nectar and moves the flower's pollen.

Part B: questions 1 and 2, in complete sentences.
Part C: your notebook page (both boxes).
C-E-R: a claim, numbers from at least two trials plus one real bird, and your reasoning.
